issues.explanation: 'Noticing Weapons' is a poor fit for the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is evidence of weapon-related assault or generalized violence cues; the rest of the profile centers on interpersonal abuse and nonspecific danger rather than weapon-focused threat monitoring, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma context.

'Inaction Guilt' is clinically questionable in this context because it implies self-blame for not doing more to stop the abuse, which is less coherent with an ongoing coercive partner-abuse formulation than appraisals centered on shame, powerlessness, betrayal, or worthlessness. It is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it stands out as weakly aligned with the trauma narrative and node pattern.

vignette:
At 51, Arun had been married for more than two decades and worked as a tax inspector, a job that once suited his careful, methodical style. The trauma he now spoke about began inside that marriage, in episodes of physical abuse by his wife that he had never imagined possible from someone he trusted. In the incident he returned to most often, though never in a complete sequence, they had been arguing late at night in the kitchen after a long workday when he was already exhausted. He remembered the sharp shift in her face when the argument turned unpredictable, the feeling of being trapped by the counter, and then only flashes: her coming toward him suddenly, the blow, the jolt of pain, the sense that he was no longer a husband in a shared home but something to be handled and overpowered. What stayed with him was not a coherent account but a few violent pieces and an enduring conviction that he had been betrayed in the place where he should have been safest.

In the weeks afterward, Arun found that tiredness made everything worse. On days when field visits ran long or he came home depleted from reviewing files, even a vague sense of discomfort or a change in plans could set off the feeling that danger was close. In restaurants and conference rooms he began choosing seats with his back to the wall so he could see the room, and in parking lots he caught himself turning to check behind him, as if someone might be approaching. The same moments also opened the door to the memory: a sudden shard of the kitchen, her movement toward him, the impact, then nothing. The fragments forced themselves in without warning and vanished just as abruptly, leaving behind the maddening awareness that there were parts he could not recover no matter how hard he tried.

Those intrusions carried their own meaning for him. Each time the memory broke through in pieces, Arun came away feeling reduced and ashamed, as though the assault had stripped him of personhood and left him an object to be acted upon. He had come to believe that being hurt by the person he trusted most said something final about his life: if betrayal could happen there, nothing good was likely ahead. That belief sharpened his reactivity. Because he was certain he had already learned, in the worst way, that safety could disappear without warning, he treated ordinary uncertainty as a threat and scanned constantly for signs he might be caught off guard again.

Over time, the scanning seemed to feed the rest of the problem. The more he checked behind him and positioned himself defensively, the more keyed up he became, and in that keyed-up state the memory was even easier to trigger. A coworker closing his office door unexpectedly, an uncomfortable pause during a home visit, the drained feeling late in the afternoon after too little sleep-any of these could bring the fragments back. Once that happened, the old conclusions returned with force: he was not really a person in other people's eyes, only someone who could be cornered and used, and the future had narrowed to endurance rather than hope.

These beliefs also changed what he noticed in daily life. Arun had become highly sensitive to feeling uncomfortable or overtired, reading both as warning signs that he was vulnerable and that something bad might happen if he let his guard down. In the office, if a meeting became unpredictable, he felt a surge of alarm and immediately tracked the exits, wanting a wall behind him. Out in the field, he sometimes lingered before entering unfamiliar businesses, unsettled by not knowing how an interaction might unfold. Those moments did not stay isolated; his own vigilance made him more aware of bodily discomfort and fatigue, and that awareness in turn made the world seem even less safe.

At home, his wife's movements in shared space had become potent cues in themselves, but even away from her, his body seemed to expect the next blow. He often reacted as if he were in danger when nothing was actually wrong. When that happened, he later berated himself for it, which only deepened the sense that his life had been permanently altered by betrayal. He did not describe elaborate avoidance so much as a constricted way of living: controlling where he sat, watching doorways, limiting situations that felt unpredictable, and arriving at work already braced. The cost had become visible. Colleagues had noticed he was distracted in meetings, and his work, which depended on calm judgment with taxpayers in tense situations, had grown harder because fatigue, discomfort, and uncertainty now carried the emotional force of warning signals.

What finally brought Arun to seek help was not a single crisis but the feeling that the circle was tightening. After a particularly long day, a routine scheduling change at work left him suddenly on edge; he checked behind him twice in the hallway, felt the memory slam into him in fragments, and spent the evening convinced that nothing in his life would ever feel normal again. He came to treatment frightened by how quickly ordinary moments could become dangerous in his mind, and by the possibility that this was now permanent. At the same time, he was hoping-carefully, not confidently-that if he could understand why exhaustion, discomfort, and unpredictability had such power over him, he might stop living as though the next attack were always about to happen.
